title: Robust progressive-resend protocol with parity micro-chunks and tool-call boundary hints
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Background:
Redwood's streaming API needs to tolerate flaky networks and intermittent client disconnects while preserving tool/function-call semantics and structured output boundaries. Existing resume approaches either rely on full retransmit (high bandwidth) or strict idempotent chunking (hard to retrofit to tool-call boundaries).

Proposal summary:
Implement a progressive-resend protocol that combines short micro-chunk sequence numbers, lightweight forward-error-correction (parity) stripes across a moving window, and explicit tool-call boundary hints embedded in SSE events. Goals: reduce resume bandwidth, preserve strong function-call/structured-output boundaries, allow graceful compatibility with older clients that expect delta/chunk framing.

Key components (implementation outline):
1) Micro-chunking & sequencing:
- Output is emitted as micro-chunks (~256-1024 bytes depending on payload profile) each stamped with: stream_seq (monotonic), micro_seq (window-local), and payload_type (text/delta/structured).
- Chunks include optional fc_hint fields when they contain or cross function-call boundaries: fc_id (UUID), fc_start:bool, fc_end:bool. This allows the client to buffer until a function-call complete event is reconstructed.

2) Parity stripes (light FEC):
- Every N micro-chunks (configurable window, default N=8) server emits one parity chunk computed as XOR over chunk payloads within that window. Parity chunks carry parity_seq and parity_window_id.
- If up to one micro-chunk in the window is lost, client can reconstruct using parity without a full resume. We prefer XOR for simplicity and CPU predictability on both CPU and GPU hosts.

3) Resume token and progressive resend negotiation:
- Resume token contains: last_ack_stream_seq, last_ack_micro_seq, last_parity_window_id, capability_flags.
- When client reconnects and sends resume token, server computes delta: which micro-seqs missing and whether parity can reconstruct. Server then sends a progressive-resend stream that includes: missing micro-chunks, reconstructed chunks (if parity used), and a compact corrective index.
- Progressive resend is rate-limited and backpressure-aware: server respects client-declared max_recv_bytes and will chunk resend into multiple resume messages if needed.

4) Tool/function-call semantics and idempotency:
- To keep function-call/nested tool boundaries intact, server guarantees that micro-chunks flagged with fc_start/fc_end are not split during progressive-resend; if a tool-call spans a parity window, server will emit an explicit fc-repair marker that instructs the client to rehydrate a single logical function-call from multiple pieces.
- Each function-call is associated with an fc_id and an optional idempotency token the client can use to deduplicate side-effects when using tool-calls through Redwood's tool invocation adapter.

5) Backwards compatibility / negotiation:
- At connection open, server emits an initial capabilities event (SSE event: capabilities) listing supported features: parity_v1, progressive_resend, fc_hints. Older clients that do not advertise support will get a compatibility-mode stream: server falls back to legacy-frag framing and disables parity by default to preserve behavior.
- A lightweight shim will translate new micro-chunks into legacy delta fragments for older clients until they upgrade.

6) Observability and metrics:
- Emit counters and histograms: resume_attempts, resume_success_rate, parity_repair_rate, avg_resume_latency_ms, tool_call_repair_rate, bytes_saved_by_parity.
- Instrument traces at the resume negotiation entry point with tags: window_id, missing_count, repaired_via_parity (bool).

Trade-offs and rationale:
- Parity (XOR) provides low-CPU, low-latency single-loss recovery but only covers up to one missing chunk per window. We prioritize simplicity and predictable CPU cost over complex Reed-Solomon schemes for now.
- Micro-chunk size is tunable because smaller chunks reduce retransmit cost but increase header overhead and metadata. We'll default to conservative sizes and provide automatic tuning (see Optimize suggestions).
- Complexity increases on server-side state (tracking parity windows per stream). We accept this for measurable customer-facing benefits (lower resume bandwidth, better perceived reliability).

Testing plan:
- Unit: parity encode/decode, micro-chunk sequencing, fc_hint handling and idempotency logic.
- Integration: simulate packet loss patterns using the in-house stream-chaos test harness; validate reconstruction rates and end-to-end function-call reassembly with the tool-runner.
- Canary: enable progressive-resend and parity on 1% of streams in a non-critical region for 72h; monitor resume_rate and CPU tail.

Rollout tasks (work items):
- Implement micro-chunk encoder/decoder and FEC parity emitter (server runtime): ENG task 1
- Add fc_hint propagation and idempotency metadata (API layer): ENG task 2
- Resume negotiation / progressive resend handler (orchestration & limits): ENG task 3
- Compatibility shim for legacy clients (translation layer): ENG task 4
- Telemetry hooks and dashboards (Console): ENG task 5
- Integration tests + chaos injection harness updates: ENG task 6

Acceptance criteria:
- Resume success rate improves by >= 30% for simulated 0.5-2% packet loss compared to baseline full retransmit in the chaos harness.
- Parity repair avoids a full resume in at least 60% of single-chunk loss windows in canary.
- Tool/function-call boundaries reconstructed correctly (no malformed JSON or truncated tool-call payloads) in 99.99% of cases in integration tests.
- Compatibility-mode clients receive identical logical outputs (allowing only differences in chunk framing) and do not regress existing SDKs.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Should we support multi-parity windows (tolerate >1 loss) for high-loss mobile networks? (cost vs benefit)
- How to best surface fc_idempotency tokens to SDKs and tool adapters for end-to-end dedupe?
- Optimal defaults for micro-chunk size per model class (chat vs embeddings vs long-form).
